q: A nightly job always does: fetch a PDF, extract fields, validate against a schema, store. A teammate proposes an agent. Best response?
options: Use an agent so it adapts to future formats
Use a fixed workflow and add a retry branch for validation failures
Use an agent with unlimited steps for robustness
Use a single call that does everything with no validation
why: The steps are known, so a workflow gives predictable cost and testing. Agent flexibility is not needed; the single call skips validation.

q: What primarily distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: Whether the model or the developer's code decides the next step
why: Both can use tools and prompts. Control flow ownership is the difference.

q: An agent loop sometimes runs 60 steps and costs 30x the median. What is the most direct first safeguard?
options: Add a max-step and token budget with a graceful partial-answer exit
why: Hard limits bound the worst case. Temperature does not prevent loops; a bigger model may cost more.

q: Which task is the best candidate for an agent?
options: Classifying support emails into five categories
Investigating a failing test across an unfamiliar repo
why: Open-ended exploration with unknown steps and a checkable result (tests) fits an agent; the others are single calls.

q: The agent forgets a user constraint stated 20 turns ago. Which component is most implicated?
why: Dropping earlier information points to context or memory handling, such as truncation without summarisation.

q: Which situation most justifies splitting into multiple agents?
options: The task is a short Q&A that fits in one prompt
You want the system to look more advanced
A research step reads dozens of long pages that would flood the main context
The steps are strictly sequential and tightly coupled
why: Context isolation is a core benefit: a sub-agent digests bulk input and returns a summary. Tightly coupled sequential steps lose information when split.

q: An orchestrator's workers return inconsistent formats, breaking synthesis. Best fix?
options: Give workers self-contained briefs with a required output schema validated on return
Use a larger model for the orchestrator
Let the orchestrator guess the format
why: Contracts on both ends make aggregation predictable. A bigger model does not remove format variance.

q: Five agents in a chain are each 90% reliable. Roughly what is end-to-end reliability, and what follows?
options: About 59%, so add validation and caps and justify each agent
why: 0.9^5 is about 0.59 (illustrative). Errors compound, which is why boundaries need validation.

q: Which is the right use of A2A rather than MCP?
options: Delegating a long-running goal to another vendor's autonomous agent
why: A2A is for agent-to-agent delegation; the other options are tool/data access, which is MCP or function calling.

q: Two parallel specialists contradict each other and one is slow. What is a sound aggregation policy?
options: Apply a timeout, surface the conflict with sources, and resolve by rule, verification or disclosure
why: Silent selection hides uncertainty; timeouts bound latency. Disclosure or verification keeps the answer trustworthy.

q: When does a hierarchical supervisor design beat a flat orchestrator?
options: When the number of workers/tools is too large for one orchestrator to choose reliably
When there is only one worker
why: Hierarchy narrows each decision but adds latency and compression, so it only pays off at scale.

q: Which reflection setup is most likely to genuinely improve code correctness?
options: Ask the model to re-read its code and say if it is right
Run tests and feed the failures back for a targeted fix
Ask the same question three times and pick the longest answer
why: External signals such as test failures give concrete defects; self-review alone often finds nothing.

q: A plan-first agent fails whenever step 1 returns unexpected data. Best fix?
options: Add a re-plan trigger when observations contradict expectations
why: Plan-first is brittle to invalidated assumptions; re-planning on contradiction addresses exactly that.

q: Each step of an agent is 90 percent reliable (illustrative). Roughly what is end-to-end success over 10 independent steps?
why: 0.9^10 is about 0.35. Errors compound multiplicatively.

q: What does ReAct provide that plain chain-of-thought does not?
options: Actions whose observations feed back into reasoning
why: ReAct interleaves tool actions and observations; CoT reasons without acting.

q: Which is the most reliable way to prevent runaway loops?
options: A prompt sentence asking for brevity
A runtime step and budget cap with graceful exit
why: Limits enforced in code hold even when the model misbehaves.

q: A team adds a critic call after every answer and cost doubles with no accuracy gain. What next?
options: Measure on an eval set and keep reflection only where it improves results
why: Reflection must justify cost with measured gains; slice by task type and drop it where it does not help.

q: What is the primary reason to adopt a graph framework over a bare tool-calling loop?
options: Explicit control flow, durable state, and interrupts for branching or long-running workflows
It is required by LLM APIs
why: Graphs add structure, persistence and observability; the model quality is unchanged.

q: Two parallel nodes append findings to `results`, but only one set survives. What is the fix?
options: Define an append/merge reducer for the key
why: The default merge is replace; a reducer combines concurrent updates.

q: A node sends an email and then calls interrupt for approval. After approval, the email goes out twice. Best fix?
options: Move the side effect after the interrupt or guard it with an idempotency flag
why: Resume re-executes the node from its start, so pre-interrupt side effects repeat.

q: Which design makes a validate-and-retry loop safe?
options: Attempt counter with cap, error fed back, and a give-up route
why: Without a cap or changed input a loop can spin forever; error feedback makes retries differ.

q: After a redeploy, users' conversations lose all history. Most probable cause?
why: In-memory savers do not survive restarts; use a durable store.

q: Which is the best debugging move for a wrong final answer in a checkpointed graph?
options: Find the first checkpoint with bad state, inspect that node, fork and re-run from before it
Re-run the whole thing hoping it changes
why: Explicit state lets you localise the first faulty step and replay from it.

q: Your agent must delete customer records when asked. Which design is best?
options: Give the tool direct delete rights with no prompt
Rely on the system prompt saying be careful
Let the model retry deletes until success
Soft delete with preview, user approval and an audit log
why: Consequential actions need approval, reversibility and auditability; prompt-only care is not enforcement.

q: Tool outputs of 30k tokens each fill the context after a few calls. Best first step?
options: Filter, limit and summarise at the tool, signalling truncation
Switch to a model with a bigger window only
Remove tool results from history entirely
why: Fix the source of bloat and tell the model what was trimmed; a bigger window is costlier and does not solve relevance.

q: Which error should be retried automatically with backoff?
why: Transient server errors are worth bounded retries; the others need a changed call or a different path.

q: Three independent lookups are needed. What is the best execution?
options: Run them sequentially in separate turns
Let the model emit all three calls in one turn and run concurrently
Merge them into one tool at random
why: Independent calls can be parallelised for latency; the runtime maps results back by call id.

q: The agent often picks tool A when B is right; both descriptions say 'searches data'. Most likely fix?
options: Lower the temperature to zero only
Differentiate descriptions with when-to-use and when-not-to-use guidance
why: Overlapping vague descriptions cause misselection; sharpen boundaries and measure.

q: In agentic tool use, which statement is correct?
options: The application executes the tool and returns the result
The model executes the function inside the provider
Tools run only once per task
why: The model only requests calls; your runtime executes, giving you control over validation and permissions.

q: Why is Python-level restricted exec() not enough for model-generated code?
options: It is not an OS-level boundary and does not limit network, CPU or memory reliably
why: Language-level blocklists get bypassed and do not enforce resource isolation; real isolation is OS/VM based.

q: Which network policy is right for a code sandbox by default?
options: Deny all, allowlist specific hosts via a proxy if needed
why: Default deny limits exfiltration and SSRF; internal and metadata addresses must stay blocked.

q: Sandboxed code prints 2GB of text. What should the harness have done?
options: Passed it all to the model
Capped output, truncated with a marker, and enforced limits while reading
why: Output caps protect memory, context and cost.

q: An agent reads untrusted web pages and also holds a send-email tool. Best mitigation?
options: Separate capabilities and require human approval for sending
why: Injected instructions in content could trigger sends; splitting duties and gating limits the blast radius.

q: Which isolation best suits running code for many untrusted tenants?
options: Ephemeral microVM or managed sandbox per run
why: Separate kernels and no shared state limit cross-tenant compromise.

q: Which best describes the N x M problem MCP addresses?
options: Each AI app needs custom code for each data source or tool
why: A shared protocol reduces N x M bespoke integrations to N clients plus M servers.

q: A stdio MCP server breaks as soon as you add debug prints. Likely cause?
options: stdout carries protocol messages and was corrupted
why: Stdio uses stdin/stdout for JSON-RPC; write logs to stderr.

q: You connect 15 MCP servers and tool selection worsens and cost rises. Best response?
options: Expose a relevant subset per task and namespace names
why: Many tool definitions bloat context and confuse selection; scope the exposed set.

q: How do MCP and tool calling relate?
options: MCP supplies and routes tools; the model still uses tool calling
why: The host converts MCP tools into model tool definitions and forwards calls over MCP.

q: Which control best reduces harm from a poisoned tool description?
options: Reviewing and allowlisting servers plus sandboxing and per-call approval
why: Layered controls on trust, privilege and consent limit what injected instructions can do.

q: A remote MCP server must serve many users with different data access. What auth approach fits?
options: Per-user authorization with scoped, validated tokens
No auth, rely on obscure URLs
why: Per-user scoped auth preserves least privilege and per-user auditing.

q: Which control guarantees a runaway agent loop stops?
options: Asking the model in the prompt to finish quickly
why: Budgets enforced by the harness cannot be ignored by the model.

q: After a crash, a resumed run sends a duplicate payment. Root cause and fix?
options: Model hallucination; use a better model
Non-idempotent step re-executed; use an idempotency key and persisted step status
why: Resume can repeat the last step; idempotency keys make repeats safe.

q: Which progress UX is best for a 4-minute agent job?
options: Streamed step events, elapsed time, background execution with notification, and cancel
why: Structured progress keeps trust; raw reasoning is not needed and may leak.

q: The agent claims it saved a record but it did not. What design change helps most?
options: Verify the real effect via tool result or read-back before reporting success
why: False success is cured by checking actual state, not the model's claim.

q: A user cancels mid-run after one irreversible action completed. Best behaviour?
options: Stop further steps and tell the user exactly what already happened
why: Cancellation cannot undo past effects; honest reporting and compensating options are required.

q: Which is a good trigger for escalating to a human?
options: Low confidence on a high-value or irreversible action after failed attempts
why: Escalate on risk and repeated failure with context handed over.

q: A user states a hard constraint early in a long chat; after summarisation the agent violates it. Best fix?
options: Keep hard constraints in pinned structured state or the system prompt
why: Pinned state survives trimming; narrative summaries are lossy.

q: Which approach handles a user changing their city best?
options: Update or supersede the old memory with a timestamp
Append the new fact and keep the old
why: Conflicting facts must be reconciled, otherwise retrieval returns contradictions.

q: Retrieval returns loosely related memories that distract the model. First adjustments?
options: Add a similarity threshold, lower k and filter by metadata
why: Precision tuning limits noise; more memories or higher k worsens it.

q: Which is a durable fact worth storing in long-term memory?
options: User's preferred programming language and deploy target
An unverified claim from a scraped web page
why: Stable, useful, verified facts merit storage; chit-chat, bulky dumps and untrusted claims do not.

q: The model is stateless. What does that imply for memory?
options: The model remembers across calls by default
Memory is built by the application choosing what to send each call
why: Everything the model 'knows' about the session is in the request, so memory is an application concern.

q: When is offloading to external storage most justified?
options: When tasks exceed the context window or need resumability
why: Add it in response to measured pressure such as overflow, large artifacts or restarts.

q: You must build a refund flow where identity verification always happens first. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Tell the agent in the prompt to verify first
Make verification a mandatory gate in code before the refund tool is reachable
why: Compliance steps belong in explicit control flow; prompts are advisory.

q: What is the key difference between a handoff and agent-as-tool?
options: Handoff transfers control to the new agent; agent-as-tool returns a result to the caller
why: The caller stays in charge with a tool call; with a handoff the receiving agent takes over.

q: Which requirement most clearly favours a graph framework over a lightweight SDK?
options: Durable resumable runs with human approval steps
why: Checkpointing and interrupts are core graph-framework strengths.

q: How best to reduce framework lock-in?
options: Keep tools as plain functions or MCP servers and prompts and evals outside the framework
why: Tools, prompts and evals port; flow logic is the costly part.

q: An agent is switched to a cheaper model and quality drops silently. What would have caught it?
options: A regression eval set run on every model change
why: Models differ in tool use and prompt sensitivity; evals reveal regressions.

q: Production runs of a long agent keep dying on deploys. Best structural fix?
options: Checkpoint each step with idempotent actions and resume in workers
why: Durable state plus idempotency lets runs resume after restarts.

q: What is the strongest reason to prefer a role-based crew over a graph for a quick content draft?
options: Speed to express a collaborative workflow where determinism is not critical
why: Role-based setups are fast to write for low-risk collaborative work; graphs fit control needs.

q: What should a user see from a long-running agent, besides the final artefact?
options: The model's full hidden chain of thought
User-safe step titles and a cancel that actually stops work
why: The contract is progress they can understand, a working cancel, and the artefact — not a leaked scratchpad.

q: Interview one-liner: when do you pick an agent instead of a workflow?
options: Whenever a framework like LangGraph is available
When the next step is unknown; use a workflow when you can write the graph
When you want lower variance and a fixed cost
why: Control-flow ownership is the test. Tools and frameworks do not make it an agent.

q: A critic pass says “think harder” with no rubric, test, or schema. What is it really?
options: A longer first pass, not a check
why: Reflection that actually checks work needs something the generator did not already see.

q: Which stop condition can the model not talk its way around?
options: A system prompt that says be concise
A runtime max-step, max-token, or max-wall-time cap
Asking the model if it is done
why: Hard stops live in the runtime. Soft advice in the prompt is not a budget.

q: The agent may draft a refund. When should the runtime execute pay()?
options: As soon as the model emits the tool call
After a second model call confirms the amount
After the user says “looks good” in free text
After an explicit approval event with an id, or a narrow logged policy
why: Consequential tools wait for a product tick, not a sentence the model interpreted as yes.

q: A search tool returns 20k tokens. What should the model see next?
options: The entire dump so nothing is lost
A short structured preview plus a store id to fetch a slice later
why: Truncate: keep a preview, persist the rest, let a later call page in.

q: When is stdio the right MCP transport, and when must you switch?
options: Stdio for a local host-spawned server; HTTP plus auth once it is remote or multi-user
HTTP for local tools, stdio for the cloud
Transport does not matter if the schema is typed
why: Stdio is a pipe to a child you own. Another machine or tenant needs a remote transport with TLS and auth.

q: A popular third-party MCP server offers a convenient “do anything” tool. First review step?
options: Install it; popularity is a review
Ask the model whether the schema looks safe
Treat it as hostile: scope tokens, review schemas, and pin what it can see
Copy its description into your system prompt
why: A server you did not write can steal credentials or inject via descriptions. Review beats a registry badge.

q: Which write belongs in long-term agent memory?
options: The full tool dump from the last search
A one-off page the user opened once
A decision, a durable preference, or an open task
why: Write an allowlist: decisions, prefs, open tasks — not every utterance.

q: A stored preference from last year now contradicts the user. What should memory do?
options: Keep it forever; history is truth
Ask the model to ignore old rows without deleting them
Expire or delete it: TTL and explicit forget are part of the design
Duplicate it so both versions stay
why: Forgetting is how memory stays correct and lawful. Every write needs a lifetime or a close event.

q: A teammate wants a five-agent crew for a task one agent with a tight tool list can do. Default?
options: Keep one agent until a bake-off shows the extra coordination is worth it
Split immediately so the system looks advanced
Add agents until each owns one sentence of the prompt
Remove all tools and hope the model plans
why: Extra agents add coordination bugs faster than quality. Defend one agent until evidence says otherwise.

q: What must a worker return so the orchestrator can merge, test, or retry?
options: A vibe such as “kind of found it”
The worker’s full chain of thought
A typed ok-plus-schema result or a typed error class and hint
why: Workers return a typed result or a typed failure. Prose cannot be merged or retried sanely.

q: Where does human approval belong in a LangGraph refund flow?
options: A comment in the prompt that says “ask first”
After the write node has already paid
An interrupt node: the graph stops, the user ticks, then the write node runs
A separate Slack bot with no graph edge
why: Approval is a node. If you cannot point to the interrupt edge, you do not have human-in-the-loop.

q: Why persist graph state after each node rather than only at the end?
options: So a crash or deploy can resume instead of restarting the whole run
So the model can see more tokens
So you can skip the saver in tests
Memory savers are enough in production
why: Checkpointing after each node is the operational rule. An in-memory saver is not persistence.

q: Generated code only needs to plot a local CSV. What is the default network policy?
options: Allow all egress so pip works
Default-deny: no egress unless the task truly needs a pin through a proxy
Let the model decide per run
why: Default-deny stops exfil and SSRF. Open a pin only when the task needs it, then close it.

q: A code-exec tool ignores wall-clock and memory caps. What can happen?
options: Nothing; the agent step budget covers it
A runaway loop can outspend the model loop and never die
why: Time and memory caps are hard kills on the runner. They sit beside the agent’s step budget.

q: A retried “create ticket” opened two tickets. What was missing?
options: An idempotency key stored by the ticket API so a replay returns the same id
A prompt that says “do not duplicate”
why: The runtime supplies a key; the API stores it. A replay must return ticket 1882 again.

q: Legal forbids streaming model thoughts. How should the UI show a four-minute run?
options: The raw tool names and arguments
User-safe step titles such as “Looking up your recent orders”
The full operator trace in the customer chat
why: Show safe titles. Operators can still open a locked trace.

q: What must a capstone demo include besides a happy-path run?
options: Step, time and cost limits, a forced-stop, and a partial artefact
Hidden thoughts streamed to the audience
why: Budgets are part of the demo. Interviewers will ask what happens at the cap; trigger it live.

q: A reviewer asks you to explain every tool call from the last run. What do you open?
options: A replayable trace: thread id, steps, redacted args, result sizes, decisions, timestamps
why: A replayable log lets you narrate the run without opening the model’s mind.
